hints: Picture the shape of benzene as a flat regular hexagon and recall what the interior angle of that geometry must be.
walkthrough:
See benzene as a flat regular hexagon**
Each carbon in benzene joins to two other carbons and one hydrogen, with all six carbons in one plane. A regular hexagon has internal angles of $120^{\circ}$, so every $\text{C-C-C}$ angle is $120^{\circ}$.

Link trigonal planar to sp2**
Three sigma bonds arranged at $120^{\circ}$ in a plane is the classic trigonal planar arrangement. That comes from $\text{sp}^2$ hybridisation, leaving one unhybridised p orbital per carbon to form the delocalised pi system above and below the ring.

hints: Recall how a halogenoalkane reacts with aluminium chloride in Friedel-Crafts alkylation to release a carbocation.
walkthrough:
Make the strong electrophile with AlCl3**
Chloroethane alone is not electrophilic enough to attack benzene. The Lewis acid catalyst $\text{AlCl}_3$ accepts $\text{Cl}^-$ from $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{Cl}$, polarising and breaking the $\text{C-Cl}$ bond. This gives the ethyl carbocation electrophile and the tetrachloroaluminate ion: $$\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{Cl} + \text{AlCl}_3 \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2^+ + \text{AlCl}_4^-$$

hints: Think where the curly arrow starts in the first step, using the electron rich pi system of benzene to attack the ethyl cation.
Draw the intermediate formed when one carbon becomes tetrahedral, showing the positive charge delocalised around the ring.
Consider how the C-H bond at the substituted carbon breaks to reform the aromatic ring and what small cation is expelled alongside ethylbenzene.
walkthrough:
Attack of the ring on the electrophile**
Benzene is electron rich because of its delocalised pi system. Draw a curly arrow from the circle, or from a $\text{C=C}$ bond, directly to the $\text{C}^+$ of $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2^+$. The pair of pi electrons forms a new $\text{C-C}$ bond to the ethyl group.

Draw the arenium intermediate correctly**
One ring carbon is now tetrahedral, bonded to H and to $\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$, and the positive charge is delocalised over the remaining five carbons. Show the intermediate as a hexagon with a broken circle or three double bonds, a + charge, with H and $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5$ on the $\text{sp}^3$ carbon.

Restore aromaticity by losing H+**
A base, often $\text{AlCl}_4^-$, removes the hydrogen from that same tetrahedral carbon. Draw a curly arrow from the $\text{C-H}$ bond back into the ring to reform the delocalised pi system. The products are ethylbenzene, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{C}_2\text{H}_5$, and $\text{H}^+$, and aromatic stability is regained which drives this step.

Final answer: Step 1: curly arrow from benzene pi bond to $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2^+$ to form arenium / Wheland intermediate with + charge in ring and $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5$ attached.
Step 2: curly arrow from C-H bond at substituted carbon back into ring to restore aromaticity.
Products: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{C}_2\text{H}_5$ + $\text{H}^+$

hints: Recall the classic test that gives a visible precipitate when free halide ions are released by hydrolysis.
walkthrough:
Choose a reagent that traps chloride**
Hydrolysis of a chloroalkane releases $\text{Cl}^-$, which gives a white precipitate with silver ions. Chlorobenzene does not hydrolyse under these mild conditions, so $\text{AgNO}_3$(aq) gives visibly different results and is ideal to show the reactivity difference.
Final answer: aqueous or alkaline $\text{AgNO}_3$ / silver nitrate

hints: Write the hydrolysis of chloroethane to ethanol plus HCl, then the precipitation step, and state what happens for chlorobenzene.
walkthrough:
Show reaction only for chloroethane**
Chloroethane undergoes nucleophilic substitution by water or hydroxide: $$\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{Cl} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH} + \text{HCl}$$ The released $\text{Cl}^-$ then precipitates: $$\text{Ag}^+ + \text{Cl}^- \rightarrow \text{AgCl}$$ seen as a white precipitate. For chlorobenzene write no equation because no hydrolysis occurs under these conditions, so no precipitate forms.

Final answer: $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{Cl} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH} + \text{HCl}$ or $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{Cl} + \text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH} + \text{NaCl}$
$\text{Ag}^+ + \text{Cl}^- \rightarrow \text{AgCl}$ white precipitate
No reaction for $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{Cl}$, no equation, no precipitate.

hints: Compare the lone pair on Cl in chlorobenzene with that in chloroethane and think how interaction with the benzene pi system changes the C-Cl bond.
walkthrough:
Explain the extra strength of aryl C-Cl**
In chlorobenzene one lone pair in a p orbital on Cl overlaps sideways with the delocalised pi system of the ring. This conjugation pulls electron density into the $\text{C-Cl}$ bond, giving it partial double bond character. The bond is therefore shorter and stronger than the $\text{C-Cl}$ bond in chloroethane, so it resists breaking by nucleophiles.

Final answer: Lone pair / p-orbital on Cl overlaps with the benzene pi system, giving the C-Cl bond partial double bond character, making it stronger and difficult to break, so nucleophilic substitution does not occur.
